A subpoena is an official legal document — issued with the authority of a court — that commands a specific person to do something in connection with a legal case. It is not a request. It is not an invitation. It is an order backed by the full power of the law.

The word is used in legal settings: courtrooms, investigations, hearings, and legal proceedings.
What Exactly Does It Order Someone to Do?

A subpoena orders a person to do one (or both) of two things:

1. Appear and testify
Show up at a specific place — usually a courtroom, a deposition room, or before a government committee — and answer questions under oath. This is the most common understanding of a subpoena.

2. Produce documents, records, or evidence
Hand over specific files, emails, financial records, medical records, messages, photographs, or any other material that is relevant to the case. The person doesn't necessarily have to appear in person — they simply must deliver the requested materials.

Some subpoenas require both: show up and bring specific items with you.

A subpoena is typically issued by:

  • A court or judge — the most common source
  • An attorney (lawyer) — in many legal systems, lawyers involved in a case have the authority to issue subpoenas without asking a judge each time
  • A government body or legislative committee — for example, a parliament or congress investigating a matter can subpoena individuals or organizations

Anyone. A subpoena can be directed at:

  • An ordinary person who witnessed something relevant
  • An expert (like a doctor or engineer) whose knowledge is needed
  • A company or organization (which must then produce records or send a representative to testify)
  • A government official
  • Even a third party who has no direct involvement in the dispute but holds relevant information (for example, a bank being subpoenaed to hand over someone's financial records)

Crucially, receiving a subpoena does not mean you are in trouble. It does not mean you are accused of anything. It simply means you have information or materials that the legal process needs. A bystander who saw an accident could be subpoenaed. A hospital could be subpoenaed to provide medical records. A friend who exchanged messages with one of the parties in a lawsuit could be subpoenaed.

Yes — absolutely. This is what makes a subpoena fundamentally different from a request or an invitation.

If you ignore a subpoena — if you fail to show up, refuse to testify, or refuse to hand over the required materials — you are committing what is called contempt of court. This is a serious legal offense. The consequences can include:

  • Heavy financial fines
  • Imprisonment
  • Other court-imposed penalties

There is, however, one important exception: a person may legally refuse to answer specific questions if answering them would force them to incriminate themselves (in countries like the United States, this is a constitutional right known as "pleading the Fifth"). A lawyer may also raise objections if a subpoena is overly broad, irrelevant, or abusive. But these are formal legal challenges — not simply ignoring the subpoena. You must respond through proper legal channels; you cannot just disregard it.
In What Situations Is a Subpoena Used?

Subpoenas appear in a wide range of legal situations:

  • Criminal trials: The prosecution or the defense may subpoena witnesses to testify, or subpoena records (phone logs, surveillance footage, financial data) to build or challenge a case.
  • Civil lawsuits: In disputes between individuals or companies (for example, a contract dispute or a personal injury lawsuit), both sides can subpoena witnesses and evidence.
  • Pre-trial depositions: Before a trial even begins, lawyers can subpoena witnesses to sit for a deposition — a formal session where the witness answers questions under oath, outside of court, and the answers are recorded.
  • Government or congressional investigations: Legislative bodies investigating matters of public concern (corruption, corporate misconduct, national security issues) can issue subpoenas to compel individuals and organizations to cooperate.
  • Grand jury proceedings: A grand jury (a panel that decides whether there is enough evidence to formally charge someone with a crime) can issue subpoenas to gather evidence during its investigation.

Imagine there is a fraud case in which a company is accused of financial wrongdoing. The investigating prosecutor may issue a subpoena to the company's bank, ordering it to hand over all financial records from the past five years. The prosecutor may also issue a subpoena to a former employee who witnessed suspicious activity, ordering that person to appear in court and testify under oath about what they saw.

The bank cannot say, "We prefer not to share that information." The former employee cannot say, "I'd rather not get involved." Both are legally bound to comply — or face serious consequences.

• A subpoena is a mandatory legal order, not a request.
  • It compels a person to testify, produce evidence, or both.
  • It is issued by courts, attorneys, or government bodies.
  • Anyone can receive one — including people who are not accused of anything.
  • Ignoring it is illegal and can result in contempt of court penalties.
  • The only way to legally push back is through formal legal objections, handled by an attorney.
